body_html:
How to think about it

Newton's first law: an object keeps its velocity unless a resultant force acts. Second law: Fnet = ma. Third law: forces come in equal and opposite pairs acting on different objects. A free-body diagram shows all the forces on one object.

Weight is Fg = mg (g = 9.8 N/kg). Friction opposes sliding: Ff = μFN, where μ is the coefficient of friction. Static friction is usually larger than kinetic friction.

Example

A 5.0 kg box has a resultant force of 20 N. What is its acceleration?

a = F ÷ m

Answer: 4.0 m/s²

Example

A 10 kg box on a flat floor has μ = 0.30. What is the friction force when it slides?

F = μmg

Answer: 29.4 N

Common mistakes

  • Drawing the reaction force on the same free-body diagram.
  • Using mass instead of weight for the normal force.
  • Thinking a moving object needs a resultant force to keep moving.
